A 15-year-old student was arrested Tuesday after threatening Martin County High School , according to the district. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. The threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office said school resource officers and Criminal Investigations Division detectives traced the message back to Taylor. During the investigation, Taylor confessed to sending the threat, according to the Sheriff's Office. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The threat was reported through FortifyFL, Principal Lori Vogel previously told families. The Sheriff's Office immediately began investigating and identified the apparent source of the message. The district notified families Tuesday that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent. The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said they can only link Taylor to this specific threat. School officials said students found to have been involved in making threats could face both school disciplinary action and legal consequences. The district also reminded families that FortifyFL is an important tool for reporting legitimate safety concerns, but knowingly submitting false information or making a false threat can have serious consequences. False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Vogel said, adding that they can cause fear, disrupt learning, and place a burden on students, families, school employees, and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said threats made anonymously, through text messages, online, or through other electronic communications, can still be traced and investigated.

Veterans and supporters at the Ardie R. Copas State Veterans Nursing Home in Port St. Lucie are raising money for resident WiFi access and a special trip to the Congressional Medal of Honor Museum in Sebring.The fundraiser, organized with support from Ardies’ Mission, includes a raffle for a Lincoln Town Car. Organizers said proceeds will help veteran residents stay connected with loved ones and experience a museum visit dedicated to honoring military service.“This is the Ardie R. Copas State Veterans Nursing Home,” said Shyrell Copas, daughter of Medal of Honor recipient Sgt. “I’m the daughter of Ardie R. That over there is my mom, Betsy. She is the wife of Ardie Copas.”Copas also shared a personal family story connected to her father’s military service.“When my dad would go out into battle, he’d grab his Betsy (his gun), and he’d go to war,” Copas said.The nonprofit is working to fund a visit for residents to the Congressional Medal of Honor Museum in Sebring.“We’re raising money for these veterans,” Copas said. “We’re hoping to get WiFi for the nursing home and also take these guys somewhere.”“That special place is called the Congressional Medal of Honor Museum in Sebring, Florida,” she added.The Ardie R. Copas State Veterans Nursing Home is a facility in the Tradition area of Port St. Lucie.“We are a 120-bed facility,” said Sherika Ayers, life enrichment program manager at the nursing home. “We currently have a waiting list. The Los Angeles Rams' dismal season opener in Australia and their proliferating injury woes were nothing Davante Adams and Matthew Stafford couldn't overcome back home with a vintage performance against the Giants.And after New York lost Jaxson Dart on the opening drive, it didn't stand a chance.Adams made eight catches for 195 yards and hauled in two of Stafford’s four touchdown passes, and the Rams welcomed Aaron Donald back to the NFL with a 28-6 victory Monday night.RELATED STORY | NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell agrees on a 4-year contract extensionStafford passed for 327 yards for the Rams (1-1), who capitalized after the Giants (1-1) lost Dart to a left knee injury on their seventh snap. Los Angeles outgained New York with 481 yards to 182, even overcoming two turnovers in a swagger-restoring blowout.“This team, we got to the confidence level that we're at because of the work we put in, and we're not going to put any governors on what we can do here,” said Adams, who had the fourth-highest yardage total of his 13-year career. “If you're trying to be great, be a Super Bowl-caliber team, you've got to hold yourself to a high standard. We can do even a little bit better than what we did, but this is on track with what we're capable of.”The Rams played without injured All-Pros Puka Nacua and Myles Garrett, but Stafford and Adams were in top form while the preseason Super Bowl favorites rebounded competently from last week’s 27-7 debacle of a Week 1 loss to the 49ers.Adams’ catches and yards receiving were both his best performances in a Rams uniform, while league MVP Stafford moved into sixth in NFL history with his 426th career TD pass, topping Philip Rivers when Adams adroitly tracked down an 11-yard fade in the third quarter.Adams was extraordinary in the second game of his 13th NFL season. He made a two-handed grab high above his head before taking it for a 31-yard touchdown on the Rams’ second possession, and he made a 64-yard catch on their third drive to set up Kyren Williams’ 10-yard TD catch.“(Adams) was special, and it showed all night,” coach Sean McVay said. “I thought he made some great plays, but you can see there's a lot of trust he and Matthew have. It's only going to continue to build, and I was really happy for him.”RELATED STORY | NFL ends the Pro Bowl game, but players will still be honored as Pro BowlersJameis Winston went 11 of 27 for 111 yards with an interception in place of Dart, who left the field shakily after taking a huge hit from Byron Young and Josaiah Stewart. The second-year quarterback, who looked great in last week's win over Dallas, watched the second half in a track suit.After his first loss with the Giants, coach John Harbaugh wouldn't confirm Dart's injury is a sprained knee ligament, but said it's “in the neighborhood of it.”“It's tough to come in, (but Winston) executed and he operated well,” Harbaugh said. “But as a group, as a team, we just didn't do what we needed to do to even have a chance to win the game. We didn't play up to that level across the board.”Winston and the Giants’ offense couldn’t get much going after Dart’s exit. Winston threw an end-zone interception to Trent McDuffie in the second quarter, and New York managed only a field goal after Jevon Holland forced and recovered a fumble at the Los Angeles 11 right before halftime, with Donald stuffing Najee Harris on a classic third-down tackle.“No excuses,” said running back Cam Skattebo, who managed only 36 yards on 12 carries. “They outperformed us, they out-executed us, and we just need to go back to the film room and fix some things.”Stafford put it away on a scoring pass to Terrance Ferguson with 8:57 to play.

Dolly Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, has reportedly been fired from his longtime role overseeing security for the late country music legend.TMZ reported on Monday that it obtained a termination notice saying Seaver and his security companies had been immediately dismissed. TMZ also reported that a new security team has already taken over at Parton’s two Nashville homes, as well as her museum and warehouse.Seaver and his team told TMZ they were “dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions.” Their statement also criticized Parton’s longtime manager, Danny Nozell, and Pinnacle Bank.“We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith, and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much,” the statement said.Seaver is the son of Parton’s sister, Cassie, and served as his aunt’s head of security for more than two decades. His father, Larry, held the role before him.Seaver was also the person who announced Parton’s death in a video posted to her Instagram account on Aug. He said in the video that Parton had asked him years earlier to make the announcement when the time came.Parton died at 80 following a brief battle with cancer.Since her death, tributes honoring Parton’s life and legacy have continued. Plans are underway to rename Nashville International Airport in her honor, and the city will celebrate its first “Dolly Day” on Sept.

Three minors have been arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old girl in Riviera Beach, according to the Riviera Beach Police Department. Marshals Service took the suspects into custody for the August 21 shooting, and all three now face first-degree murder charges. Riviera Beach Police Chief Michael A. Coleman held a press conference Tuesday morning to provide more details on the case."This was a heartbreaking loss for her family, her friends, and our community," Coleman said. "According to our investigation, three juveniles allegedly planned to rob the victim of a firearm she attempted to sell. That attempted robbery escalated into violence, and a young life was cut short."WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW: Officers responded to the 1400 block of West 36th Street near Goodmark Park shortly after 8 p.m. and discovered the victim suffering from a gunshot wound to the head. Police determined the suspects, who knew the victim from the community but were not friends, communicated with her through social media to arrange the gun sale before attempting to rob her instead.The alleged shooter, a 17-year-old, faces first-degree premeditated murder with a firearm, principal in the first degree, and tampering with a witness, victim, or informant. Two accomplices, both 16, each face first-degree murder, principal in the first degree, and attempted armed robbery charges.One suspect was arrested in Jacksonville while two were taken into custody in Riviera Beach. Two of the three juveniles were previously known to law enforcement and had been in the system for several years, Coleman said.Advanced surveillance technology proved crucial in solving the case. Detectives used Flock camera and License Plate Reader technology to track the suspect vehicle as it fled the scene immediately after the shooting, following it to the suspects' homes.Coleman added that the department will continue using Flock cameras despite recent state restrictions on their use on state roads."We'll continue to use the Flock cameras until they go away, until the city leadership decide they don't no longer want them in the city," Coleman said. "They're invaluable to our investigation, how we use them."Coleman emphasized that the investigation remains active and additional arrests may be forthcoming. He also addressed the broader issue of youth violence plaguing the community."We've experienced a lot of activity like this in our community for many, many years, and we're starting to move forward, not just in this community, throughout Palm Beach County to plan together to address youth violence," Coleman said. Pastor Tony Drayton, a community leader who has worked for years to address violence in the area, joined Coleman at the press conference. "Our community has been bruised. Our community has been damaged," Drayton said. "And I do believe that just because we're bruised and damaged doesn't mean that we're at the point of failure. There's still hope."The three juveniles are being held at the Juvenile Assessment Center and have not been charged as adults. Coleman said the legal process will determine if they should be tried as adults based on state statutes.Coleman stressed that despite this incident, Riviera Beach remains a safe place to visit and live. "This is not a black eye or blemish on what all the great work we have done in this city," Coleman said. "Riviera Beach is a place that I consider a great place, and I want everybody outside of Riviera Beach to feel it's a great place to come and enjoy the beaches that we have and our communities."The investigation remains active. Anyone with additional information is urged to contact the Riviera Beach Police Department at 561-845-4123 or submit an anonymous tip through Crime Stoppers at 1-800-458-TIPS (8477).

Many Florida drivers may not know it is illegal to use the far-left lane as a general travel lane — and a viewer's frustration sparked a test of just how well people know the law.Kevin Eddy drives from Stuart to Palm Beach County every day and said left-lane drivers are causing unwanted congestion on the roads. His concern prompted a closer look at what Florida law actually requires.Florida law requires drivers to use the far-left lane mainly for passing and not as a general travel lane. The rule applies to roads with a speed limit of 65 mph or higher.WATCH BELOW: Florida's left-lane law has drivers guessing — here's what you need to knowWhen asked whether they knew it was illegal to drive in the left lane, some drivers admitted they did not."I did not know," Alfredo Milian said."I call it a gray area, but yes," another driver said."I've heard about it, that it's illegal to. Or you're not supposed to drive in the left lane for a long period of time, always driving the right lane," a third driver said.Eddy said better signage and stronger enforcement could help."You really don't have hardly any signs at all," Eddy said."And you also have to realize we have a lot of tourists here, so we have a lot of people that aren't familiar with the laws in Florida," Eddy said.There are exceptions to the left-lane rule during heavy traffic congestion, but experts say drivers should always merge back to the right after passing another car.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A long-running legal fight over Missouri’s congressional map took another turn Monday when a federal appeals panel ruled in favor of new districts backed by President Donald Trump, even though the U.S. Supreme Court has blocked those districts from being used in the November election.A three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said Missouri should use the new Republican-drawn U.S. House districts in the November election, just as the state did in its August primary. To revert to its prior districts for the general election would violate the U.S. Constitution, the appeals judges said.The appeals panel directed a lower court judge to issue a permanent injunction against using anything other than the map favored by Trump. But the ruling has no immediate impact. That’s because the panel also ordered the judge to delay the effect of the order for one week to allow time for an appeal. The judge quickly did so.Opponents of the new map said Monday that they will file an emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.The Supreme Court already has twice sided against the Trump-backed map. Earlier this month, it blocked enforcement of a lower court order favoring the new map pending a potential appeal and eventual decision by the high court.Missouri currently is set to run its November election with the same congressional districts it used in 2024 and 2022, following prior decisions by both the Missouri Supreme Court and the U.S. Supreme Court.Appeals panel ruling comes amid absentee votingLocal elections officials already have sent absentee ballots to overseas citizens and military voters using the 2022 districts. State law requires absentee ballots to be available to all other voters by Tuesday.Local elections officials theoretically could scramble to change ballots again and could send replacements for ones already distributed. But if voters already have cast an absentee ballot, they cannot change their vote — even if the district boundaries have changed.Miller County Clerk Clinton Jenkins said he mailed an absentee ballot Friday to a Missouri voter living in Australia and also sent ballots to other overseas voters. But he suggested that other people “wait a little deeper into the absentee period, just in case” the congressional district boundaries get swapped again.To try to change districts at this late date would be “practically impossible” and cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, the Missouri Association of County Clerks and Election Authorities had told appeals judges in a legal filing.But an attorney representing Republicans who sued — including U.S. Rick Brattin, a congressional candidate — suggested during arguments last Thursday that there still is time to revert to the Trump-backed map.The appeals panel agreed, pointing to other cases in which courts have ordered changes after absentee ballots already had been distributed to overseas citizens and military voters.The group People Not Politicians, which spearheaded a referendum petition to put the new map to a statewide vote on the November ballot, said it will appeal the latest decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.RELATED STORY | Missouri court blocks Trump-backed US House map and orders it to be put to a vote“Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted. Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said in a statement. “Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections.”Court ruling highlights constitutional conflictThe 8th Circuit decision puts the federal court at odds with Missouri's top court.“The Constitution does not permit Missouri to use a different congressional district map in the November 2026 general election than it used in the August 2026 primary election,” the appeals panel wrote in its decision.The panel consists of Judge James Loken, an appointee of former President George H.W. Bush, and two appointees of Trump — Judges David Stras and Justin Smith. Prior to his June appointment, Smith was an attorney who represented Trump as he unsuccessfully appealed a $5 million jury verdict in a lawsuit filed by the writer E. Supreme Court.Earlier this month, the Missouri Supreme Court said the state forbids the use of districts passed last September because opponents submitted thousands of petition signatures in December calling for a statewide vote on the new districts.Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins waited until August — on the same day that the primary was held under the new districts — to reject the petition. He asserted that referendum petitions aren’t allowed for congressional redistricting.The Missouri Supreme Court reversed Hoskins’ finding, ruling that the state must use the districts approved in 2022 for the November election. The high court then temporarily held Hoskins in contempt when he directed local election officials to use the 2025 map after a federal district court order favoring it.Missouri's redistricting targets Kansas CityThe new congressional map backed by Trump significantly reshapes a Kansas City-based district held by Democratic Rep. Republicans hope the map could help them win seven of the state’s eight House seats — one more than they currently hold.Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary, and Brattin won a multi-way Republican primary. Brattin praised Monday's appeals panel decision, saying that switching districts after the primary “defies common sense and undermines the entire electoral process.”RELATED STORY | Midterm voting picks up amid massive shifts in voting districtsAbout 59% of the 5th District's potential voters are new under the revised map, which also changes several other districts. All told, more than a million potential Missouri voters, or nearly 1 in 4 voters statewide, are affected by the redistricting, according to an Associated Press estimate.Missouri’s redistricting battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their U.S. House districts over the past year. Districts are usually redrawn at the start of each decade, after a census. But Trump spurred a spate of mid-decade redistricting last year when he urged Republican-led states to redraw districts to gain an edge in the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

Lucie County staff found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without a permit, and the county says it does not know who owns them. Staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night in an update on the board's Sept. 1 decision to remove automated license plate readers from county-controlled property. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14, and the search is not finished. County commissioner James Clasby says the issue isn't as much about the cameras as who's receiving the data. Not knowing who they belong to, I think, is another issue. Perhaps that goes about the entirety of Flock camera reform, Clasby said. "There's the potential for non-law enforcement to have cameras out there, and I'm not okay with that. Because the county has no permit on file for those cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. "It's like a bright red notice that says you have 30 days to remove this. And we will also bag the cameras so they're not operable," said interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations. See also: Florida boaters rescued after capsized vessel leaves them stranded in tree The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. The report says that step was meant both to give the agencies advance notice and to let them review the data for accuracy. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review. Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. The vote went beyond a state order that applies only to state highways. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes, and Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

A Fort Pierce man was arrested after a raid Friday by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service found a massive amount of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, worth several million dollars. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Special Investigations Division, with assistance from the SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant at a residence in the 3100 block of S. 24th Street in Fort Pierce. The subject of the investigation, Tony Saunders, 48, was taken into custody. Saunders, a three-time convicted felon who is on federal probation, also had two active warrants related to the sale and delivery of controlled substances. Afterward, Saunders faced additional charges of trafficking in fentanyl, trafficking in cocaine, trafficking in MDPV, manufacturing cocaine, tampering with evidence and possession of marijuana with intent to sell. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0j4igLYhtX4QpfPCZhHkYeREcfiqd9eehsAoAcjVwDWTipnXHZNWyrJLe6gbwukcvl The search resulted in the seizure of approximately 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 303 grams of cocaine, 97 grams of marijuana laced with MDPV, and 60 oxycodone pills totaling approximately 6.2 grams, the sheriff's office said. The street value of 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl can range from $150,000 to nearly $1.8 million, depending heavily on its purity, geographic location, and whether it is sold as wholesale powder or broken down into counterfeit pills, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The estimated street value of 303 grams of cocaine in the U.S. ranges between roughly $18,180 and $60,600. Detectives also seized assorted ammunition, drug paraphernalia and materials consistent with the preparation and distribution of narcotics. A single kilogram of fentanyl has the potential to kill 500,000 people, making 4.5 kilograms a lethal volume capable of millions of fatal doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. “4.5 kilos of fentanyl are 4.5 kilos that will not reach our streets," Sheriff Richard Del Tro said. "Fentanyl is a deadly poison, and those who traffic in it are putting lives at risk for profit. I commend our detectives, SWAT Team, and the U.S. Marshals Service for their commitment to this mission. We will continue to pursue those who traffic dangerous narcotics and do everything within our authority to make St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Molly’s House in Stuart is celebrating 30 years of providing affordable lodging and support services for patients and families receiving medical treatment on the Treasure Coast.The nonprofit organization, located in Stuart's medical district, was founded to help families stay close to doctors, hospitals and treatment providers during difficult medical situations. Leaders with Molly's House said the mission continues to focus on reducing stress for families facing long-term care and recovery.WATCH BELOW: Molly’s House celebrates 30 years in StuartKate Wiegerink, a member of the Molly’s House board of directors and Molly Sharkey's sister, said the organization also works to educate new doctors, nurses and community members about the services available to patients and families."We want people to know these resources exist," Wiegerink said during the anniversary celebration.Molly's House provides affordable lodging for guests traveling for treatment and also offers a free cancer support program for residents, according to organization leaders.The nonprofit is celebrating the milestone with an open house Monday at its facility on Osceola Street in Stuart. Community members are invited to tour the house and healing garden while learning more about the organization’s history and programs.Brandi Patricio, whose son TJ (Timothy) is receiving treatment, shared how the nonprofit has helped her family manage the financial and emotional challenges tied to ongoing medical care.Patricio said having access to affordable lodging reduces anxiety about housing costs during treatment and allows families to focus on recovery and care.In addition to housing support, Molly's House provides weekly free meals to residents to help ease food expenses and preparation during stressful medical situations. Businesses and individuals can become a "Chef for a Day" and provide an average of 28 meals.The organization’s leaders said demand for support services remains strong as more families seek affordable options near treatment centers across South Florida and the Treasure Coast.Click here for more information about Molly’s House and its programs.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The San Francisco 49ers handled the return from Australia just as well as the trip there and have started the season with two convincing victories.Christian McCaffrey became the fourth-fastest player in the Super Bowl era with 100 career touchdowns, Brock Purdy played a near-perfect game and the 49ers overwhelmed the Miami Dolphins 35-13 on Sunday.The 49ers showed no signs of fatigue after beating the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in the opener in Australia and began the season with back-to-back wins of at least 20 points for the first time in franchise history."That's what I was real proud of the guys," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "That was the biggest challenge of this, just the human nature of what all went into Week 1 and the travel and everything and coming back after five days off. But we got a really cool team in terms of how much guys care about football how into it they are."The 49ers scored touchdowns on their first five drives and dominated the Dolphins, who spent the week since losing the opener in Las Vegas by practicing in nearby Napa.Avoiding the travel was little help to an overmatched Miami team that came into the season with a record of more than $180 million in dead money on the salary cap.Purdy went 20 for 22 for 287 yards, two touchdown passes and one TD run, completing 18 straight passes at one point. He connected on a 12-yard touchdown pass to George Kittle and a 6-yarder to Kyle Juszczyk on the first two drives of the third quarter to break the game open."For me, every play, every drive mattered. It wasn't like we went out there and just blew these guys out. That where my head space was at. How can I move the ball, take the right looks and keep us ahead of the chains. That's what my mindset is at."McCaffrey scored on a pair of 1-yard runs to give him 100 touchdowns in 114 games, with only LaDainian Tomlinson (89 games), Emmitt Smith (93) and Shaun Alexander (96) getting their faster in the Super Bowl era.McCaffrey, who has 50 touchdowns with both Carolina and San Francisco, joined Marshall Faulk and Randy Moss as the only players to score at least 50 TDs with two franchises."It's kind of crazy to hear that," McCaffrey said. "I watched all those guys growing up. Marshall Faulk was somebody that I've probably seen every single snap he's played. I don't take it for granted. Randy Moss I played with a ton of time with Madden growing up. Those are huge, huge honors."Malik Willis went 14 for 23 for 197 yards for Miami but took four sacks and was unable to lead a touchdown drive until his 77-yard pass to Ryan Miller with 2:30 remaining in the game."They've got great players who are experienced and have been running this system for a very long time," said Miami coach Jeff Hafley, who was an assistant for the 49ers in Shanahan's first two seasons in 2017-18. "When I saw Kittle and Juice after the game, they were here when I was here in 2017. So great players, great play-caller, consistency and continuity in one scheme over time usually equals success. That's a really good team."Both defenses struggled to get off the field in the first half with the main difference being the Niners finished off their drives with touchdowns. Riley Patterson missed a 51-yard field goal on Miami's opening drive and the Dolphins settled for two field goals in the red zone on their other two possessions in the first half.San Francisco got in the end zone with McCaffrey scoring on a 1-yard run and Purdy on a 2-yard run on the two drives for the 49ers, who led 14-6 at the half.Dolphins: RB Jaylen Wright (stinger) left in the first half. WR Caleb Douglas (ankle) left in the second half.49ers: WR Demarcus Robinson and DT James Thompson Jr. left with what Shanahan believes were high ankle injuries and could miss some time. WR Mike Evans left in the second half with a hip injury but likely could have returned if the game had been closer.Dolphins: Host Kansas City on Sunday.49ers: Host Arizona on Sunday.

A proposed luxury waterfront development in Fort Pierce is drawing renewed attention after city commissioners approved a motion to explore hiring outside legal counsel to review whether the city has any options to challenge the project under Florida's Live Local Act. 14 vote comes as cities across Florida continue testing the limits of the state's Live Local Act and lawmakers implement the latest round of changes to the law. The proposed Causeway Cove development on South Hutchinson Island has become one of the Treasure Coast's most closely watched growth disputes, putting residents and local officials at odds with a state law that limits how much control cities have over certain housing projects. 14 meeting, the commission approved a motion to explore hiring an outside land-use attorney to determine whether Fort Pierce has any legal grounds to challenge the project under the Live Local Act. The city is also monitoring lawsuits filed elsewhere in Florida that seek to restore greater local control over development decisions. The move comes as Florida enters the latest phase of the law. Known as Live Local 4.0, the most recent changes took effect July 1, 2026, expanding eligible development sites and further clarifying protections for qualifying projects that include affordable housing. Qualifying developments must continue to reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years. Now, Fort Pierce finds itself at the center of a broader statewide debate over growth, affordable housing and home rule. The proposed redevelopment would dramatically transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive. According to city records, plans call for five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips. For residents like Edie Harrison, the project would change the area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems." Harrison and hundreds of other residents have raised concerns about the size of the development, traffic impacts and what they view as a lack of public input. At the center of the fight is Florida's Live Local Act, a law passed in 2023 to encourage the construction of affordable and workforce housing across the state. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the law and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. For critics, that process has become one of the most controversial aspects of the proposal. Fort Pierce Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. Critics argue the formula can produce rents that technically qualify as affordable under state guidelines but remain difficult for many local residents to afford. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city. Even some lawmakers who supported the legislation have raised concerns about how it is being applied. Dana Trabulsy, whose district includes parts of the Treasure Coast, has recently questioned whether developments of this scale reflect what legislators intended when they approved the measure. The Fort Pierce dispute is also part of a much larger battle unfolding across Florida. Several lawsuits challenging aspects of the Live Local Act are moving through the courts as cities seek to regain greater authority over local development decisions. Supporters of the law argue it is helping address Florida's housing shortage, while critics contend it has weakened local home-rule powers and limited communities' ability to shape growth. Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida , making the law one of the most significant growth and housing measures enacted in recent years. Related 2024 article: $100M Kanner Hwy development in Stuart: Affordable housing powered by Live Local Act If things move forward as anticipated, construction on the Causeway Cove development could begin before the end of the year. The property's owner, Palm Beach developer Ashton DePeyster, did not respond to requests for comment. This report is part of an ongoing CBS12 News I-Team investigation examining the impact of Florida's Live Local Act, the legal challenges surrounding the law, and how communities across the Treasure Coast are responding to large-scale development projects.

Lucie road rage incident that escalated into a physical fight and shooting landed two men in handcuffs Thursday. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Police said that before the shooting, one driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. Investigators determined there was no intentional following, police said. One of the drivers, identified as Tylon Kukielka, 57, was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as Dean Plotts, 41, was traveling in the same direction. Police said the situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace. During the fight, Kukielka allegedly fired his gun, striking Plotts twice in the left wrist and legs. See also: Formerly conjoined twins see each other face-to-face after historic separation surgery A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Detectives later charged Kukielka with attempted homicide. Plotts was charged with burglary with assault or battery. Both men were taken into custody. The incident remains under investigation.

38-year-old Darrel Abbey is facing multiple charges after Martin County deputies say he barricaded himself inside a Palm City guest house during an hours-long standoff with law enforcement Saturday . According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Abbey was taken into custody after SWAT officers and hostage negotiators spent hours trying to convince him to surrender. Deputies said they were initially called to a home along SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road for a domestic-related incident. Investigators say the situation escalated when Abbey, who deputies say was armed and dangerous and under the influence of alcohol, barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property. "I was pretty scared because it doesn't usually happen in our neighborhood," said 11-year-old Gavin Ryan, who lives next door. See also: Routine warrant leads to shocking major animal cruelty bust in Lake Worth Ryan's mother said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard several gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard. SWAT officers later positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded. Deputies said hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to get Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported. Another neighbor, Julian Tracy, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. "[Gavin's] mom told me about it, and I was like, 'Whoa,' Tracy said. "I've never heard about a shooting in someone's neighborhood." Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail and is facing three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Jail records show he is being held on a $12,500 bond.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

hero.headline: Fort Pierce brothers killed in Georgia shooting; suspect arrested after football game altercation
hero.body:
An 18-year-old suspect has been arrested in connection with the shooting deaths of two Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, who were killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the deaths of Jamarion Rolle, 11, and Ja'khi Clark, 12.

According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys said the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Both survived and received treatment for their injuries. One of the women underwent surgery on Thursday.

The boys grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt said both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother said they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family.

"Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society."

The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida for burial.
hero.article_text: Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. hero.headline: Three severe hoarding cases in Martin and Palm Beach counties this summer spark debate over prevention
hero.body:
Three animal hoarding cases this summer in Martin and Palm Beach counties have prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent animal neglect before it reaches a crisis point. On July 20, Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound. Exactly three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. On Sept. 16, Palm Beach County deputies serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana rescued 13 dogs from another feces-filled home, with seven of the dogs confined inside two cages.

The answers to preventing such cases are not simple, experts say. A major obstacle is the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek addressed the limitation when initially asked about the border collie case, after a neighbor raised concerns about the dogs.

"There's laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause," Budensiek said.

That constitutional boundary makes the problem difficult to address through legislation alone. Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals, works in Tallahassee to help shape animal welfare policy.

"Our legislators are filing more animal bills," MacFall said. "We've done a lot of really good things in recent years, but there's a lot of work to be done."

Preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated, MacFall said.

"It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said.

Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are not unusual.

"Unfortunately, it's really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on," Perea said.

Perea pointed to intent gone wrong when asked why such cases are common.

"It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong," Perea said.

Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing, but that public awareness is.

"I don't know if it's so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we're experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it," Perea said.

For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool.

"If you see something, say something. I mean, that's for a reason," MacFall said.

Some policy efforts are in the works. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. In Palm Beach County, commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall.

hero.headline: Stolen Broward deputy patrol car tracked to I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after authorities tracked a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle to Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in St. Lucie County and established a perimeter with K-9 units and drones over concerns the suspect had access to a firearm.

Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale, was detained after deputies spotted her wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Broward County Regional Communications had received a report shortly after 9 p.m. that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale.

Investigators working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95. Port St. Lucie police officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm.

"The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources."

Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence.

She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators.

The Broward County Sheriff's Office said nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty and reported his marked unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated.

Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested under hotel bed faces meth, child neglect charges
cards.teaser: Kenneth Robert Ferow II, wanted on a Martin County warrant, was arrested at a Port St. Lucie hotel where officers found him hiding under a bed with methamphetamine and two children in the room.
cards.body:
Kenneth Robert Ferow II, wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant, now faces additional charges of methamphetamine possession and two counts of child neglect after Port St. Lucie police found him hiding under a hotel bed with two children present in the room.

Officers went to a hotel on Village Parkway on Tuesday after receiving information that Ferow, 41, was inside a room. Ferow's wife told officers he was not there, according to Port St. Lucie police.

Officers said they had credible information Ferow was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room. Officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there.

Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident. Officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine. Two children, ages 14 and 8, were inside the hotel room at the time. Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding warrant.

hero.headline: Two major Martin County animal hoarding rescues prompt scrutiny of prevention gaps
hero.body:
Two animal hoarding rescues in Martin County this summer removed more than 130 animals within three weeks and drove new questions about whether prevention efforts can stop neglect before it reaches crisis levels. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek called the first rescue the worst hoarding case he had seen, and the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast later said the second was the worst they had ever encountered.

Deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound on July 20. Three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. A third hoarding case emerged Sept. 16 in Palm Beach County, where deputies serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana rescued 13 dogs from a feces-filled home. Seven of the dogs were confined inside two cages, according to the affidavit.

Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said the level of neglect is common throughout the country. He attributed the cases to good intentions that eventually go wrong, whether in breeding operations or rescue operations. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing, but that public awareness is increasing through social media and greater community involvement.

Kate MacFall, Florida state director for Humane World for Animals, said legislators are filing more animal bills and recent years have brought progress, but preventing hoarding cases specifically remains complicated. Budensiek pointed to the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures as a major obstacle, noting that law enforcement faces strict limits on probable cause. Perea cautioned that legislation can create unintended consequences. MacFall said individual action remains the most effective tool, urging people to report concerns when they see them.

Some policy efforts are moving forward. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. Palm Beach County commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall.

cards.headline: Stolen Broward deputy's patrol vehicle tracked to I-95 in St. Lucie County, Fort Lauderdale woman arrested
cards.teaser: A Fort Lauderdale woman faces multiple felony charges after authorities tracked a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle to Interstate 95 near Port St. Lucie Tuesday night and established an armed-suspect perimeter.
cards.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman faces multiple felony charges after authorities tracked a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle to Interstate 95 near Port St. Lucie Tuesday night and established an armed-suspect perimeter. Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale, was arrested along the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Lucie after deputies spotted her wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.

Port St. Lucie police officers established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. The department deployed both K-9 units and drone resources during the search. Drone video shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident.

Broward County Regional Communications received a report shortly after 9 p.m. Tuesday that a marked Broward Sheriff's Office vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators worked with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office to track the vehicle to St. Lucie County. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said.

Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty and reported his marked unit missing. The Broward Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested under hotel bed faces meth, child neglect charges
cards.teaser: Kenneth Robert Ferow II, wanted on a Martin County battery warrant, was arrested at a Village Parkway hotel where police found him hiding under a bed with methamphetamine and two children in the room.
cards.body:
Kenneth Robert Ferow II, wanted on a Martin County battery warrant, was arrested at a Port St. Lucie hotel Tuesday where police found him hiding under a bed with methamphetamine in his possession and two children in the room. The 41-year-old now faces new charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect in addition to the outstanding warrant.

Port St. Lucie police officers went to a hotel on Village Parkway after receiving information that Ferow was inside a room. Ferow's wife told officers he was not there, but officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room.

Officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there. Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident.

Officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine. Two children, ages 14 and 8, were also inside the hotel room at the time of the arrest.

hero.headline: Arsenic hot spot found on Fort Pierce brownfield, not Shelli development site
hero.body:
New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the waterfront land the city sold to developer Chris Shelli. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of a former citrus packing house property. That hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli. His proposed development property sits across the street.

The distinction undercuts a key argument Fort Pierce has made in the developer's pending breach-of-contract lawsuit. In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was likely contaminated and that the cost of remediation essentially eliminates his damages claim. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels associated with the former citrus packing house property but did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.

FDEP did find arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli, but both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target. Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, reviewed the findings and said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. Beckler noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils.

Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman's Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination. Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development. Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023, about two years after the sale, that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million. In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli. The city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected.

A city spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.

However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: South Florida Water Management District could lose $98 million annually by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes
hero.body:
The South Florida Water Management District could lose approximately $98 million in annual revenue by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes, according to data presented this week at Stuart City Hall. Amendment 3 would reduce property tax revenue that funds waterway protection projects in Florida.

Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard told the Rivers Coalition that water quality projects protecting the St. Lucie Estuary would be affected by the funding loss. "The projects that improve water quality, that improve stormwater treatment, will be impacted, will be defunded," Heard said.

Mark Perry, president of the Rivers Coalition, said local projects funded by property tax revenue include retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems that remove nitrogen and phosphorus to prevent algae blooms. The Rivers Coalition works to protect the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon.

"What you have to do is evaluate. I'm going to get, reduce my tax liability over the next few years with this amendment. But is that worth the services that are going to be reduced?" Perry said during the meeting.

Environmental policy adviser Eric Draper spoke to the coalition about how reduced property tax revenue could affect water management districts responsible for water supply, flood control and water quality. Perry said passage of Amendment 3 would force local governments to decide whether to cut back on water quality projects or find alternative funding sources.

"We're going to have a growing state and growing community here with growing runoff. That is going to happen," Perry said.

A board member from the South Florida Water Management District told the Rivers Coalition that if Amendment 3 passes, it would affect the next fiscal year's budget, not the current one. The board member could not specify which projects might be impacted.

Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard expressed concern about the potential impact on water quality projects. Perry explained that local projects funded by property tax revenue, such as retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems, play a vital role in improving water quality by removing elements like nitrogen and phosphorus, which can prevent algae blooms. cards.teaser: A barn fire on a ranch near Indiantown Thursday evening destroyed the structure and about six vehicles. One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms.
cards.body:
A barn fire on a ranch in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown destroyed the structure and about six vehicles Thursday evening, according to Martin County Fire Rescue.

The fire occurred at about 5:30 p.m. and produced large flames and black smoke visible for miles. No horses or residents were injured. One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms but was released Friday morning.

The barn and about six vehicles were a total loss, including a side-by-side and a small front-loader tractor. Southwest Allapattah Road reopened after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

hero.headline: Brightline files for bankruptcy, secures $490 million investment to keep South Florida-Orlando trains running
hero.body:
Brightline filed for bankruptcy and secured a $490 million long-term capital investment to keep trains running between South Florida and Orlando while the high-speed rail service reorganizes its debt and pursues profitability. The restructuring comes after Brightline struggled to meet revenue projections despite growing ridership.

Patrick Goddard, chief executive officer of Brightline Florida, said the transaction will be a catalyst for further growth in ridership and revenue.

Brightline reported a 17 percent increase in revenues in 2026 over the previous year. Analysts said the high-speed rail had difficulty meeting projections based on the number of riders and revenue per rider.

Tim Hynes, Global Head of Research for Debtwire, said the restructuring can allow Brightline to focus on being profitable. Hynes said success will require a combination of raising rates and getting more people to use the service, but he believes the rail will be successful over the long haul.
