The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said that second case was the worst hoarding case they had ever seen.

Budensiek addressed the constitutional limitation when a neighbor raised concerns about the border collies at a community meeting. "There's laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause," Budensiek said. The Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures remains a major obstacle to earlier intervention.

Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals, said legislators are filing more animal bills and Florida has made progress in recent years. But preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated, she said. "It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said. Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said legislation can create unintended consequences. "A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful," Perea said.

Perea said cases like the Martin County rescues are common throughout the country. "Unfortunately, it's really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on," Perea said. He said hoarding cases typically start with good intentions in breeding or rescue operations that eventually go wrong. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is growing, but that public awareness is increasing through social media.

Some policy efforts are underway. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. Palm Beach County commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall. For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool. "If you see something, say something. I mean, that's for a reason," MacFall said.

cards.body:

hero.headline: Parking dispute led to Pollo Tropical shooting in Port St. Lucie, witnesses say
hero.body:
A shooting at a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie last weekend began as a dispute over a parking space, according to witness accounts in the incident report. Christopher Harris, 37, was shot in the chest but now faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon despite being listed as a victim in the report.

Multiple witnesses gave conflicting accounts of the confrontation. One witness sitting at a table inside the restaurant told police he saw Harris push another man outside and heard a verbal argument before the man discharged a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris then came back inside and asked someone to call 911.

Another witness picking up an Uber order said she saw a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. She said the man began yelling, and as she exited Pollo Tropical, she observed the man following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. The witness said she observed something in the man's hand and saw him lunge so close to the other person that they were almost touching before the other person pulled out a firearm and shot.

A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to come outside. Harris held the door open and then approached the man before the witness heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris ran up on him with a knife.

Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed that Harris faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, Palm Beach voters to decide eight local ballot questions Nov. 3
hero.body:
Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments. Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Lucie and designated portions of St. Lucie County.

Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds, repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens, expand sports complexes, improve beach access and trail connections, and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities, also repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County's existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending.

Martin County's local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve.

St. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Port St. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee. The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents' preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. The third St. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy.

hero.headline: Three major animal hoarding rescues in weeks expose legal limits on prevention
hero.body:
Three major animal hoarding rescues on the Treasure Coast and in Palm Beach County within two months have exposed the constitutional and legal limits that prevent authorities from intervening before neglect reaches crisis levels. Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a Hobe Sound house on July 20, then 36 border collies from a Palm City home on Aug. 10. On Sept. 16, Palm Beach County deputies serving an unrelated arrest warrant rescued 13 dogs from a feces-filled home near Lantana, where seven of the dogs were confined inside two cages.

The Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures remains a major obstacle to prevention efforts. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek addressed the limitation when a neighbor raised concerns about the border collies at a community meeting. "There's laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause," Budensiek said.

Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are common throughout the country. "It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong," Perea said. "A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful."

Palm Beach County commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall. Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals, said legislators are filing more animal bills but acknowledged that preventing hoarding cases specifically is complicated. "It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said. For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool. "If you see something, say something," MacFall said.

Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing but that public awareness is. "I don't know if it's so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we're experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it," Perea said.

I mean, that's for a reason," MacFall said.Some policy efforts are in the works. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. hero.source_summary: Two high-profile animal hoarding cases in Martin County this summer and a third in Palm Beach County have prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent animal neglect before it reaches a crisis point. The answers, experts say, are not simple. On July 20, Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound. 'This is the worst animal hoarding case that I've seen,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the scene. Exactly three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which was still handling rescue efforts of the previous case, then said this was the worst hoarding case they'd ever seen. On Sept. 16, Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputies, serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana, rescued 13 dogs from another feces-filled home. According to the affidavit, seven of the dogs were confined inside 2 cages. Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are not unusual. 'Unfortunately, it's really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on,' Perea said. When asked why it is so common, Perea pointed to intent gone wrong. 'It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong,' Perea said. The American Humane Society monitors cases like these across the U.S. and assists law enforcement and local animal rescues when called upon. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing but that public awareness is. 'I don't know if it's so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we're experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it,' Perea said. MacFall works in Tallahassee, where her job is to help shape Florida's animal welfare policy. 'Our legislators are filing more animal bills,' MacFall said. 'We've done a lot of really good things in recent years, but there's a lot of work to be done.' But preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated. cards.body:

One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms but was released Friday morning. Southwest Allapattah Road is back open after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce brothers killed in Georgia shooting; 18-year-old arrested after altercation
hero.teaser: The Fort Pierce community is raising money to bring home two brothers, ages 11 and 12, who were shot and killed Sunday in DeKalb County, Georgia. Police arrested an 18-year-old suspect and said the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began during a backyard football game days earlier.
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce community is raising money to bring home two brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the deaths of 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark.

According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys said the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident and both survived. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday.

The brothers grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt said both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother said they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family.

A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida to be laid to rest. DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said no family should have to endure the senseless loss of children. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. Padrick said two children should still be alive today. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support as the investigation continues in Georgia.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings that struck occupied homes
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects.

The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. No one was hurt, but several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Evidence shows all three shootings are related, police said.

"The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

Officers responded to one home around 9:07 p.m. Friday and found multiple bullet holes outside, with several rounds entering through walls and windows. At least 10 bullet holes were visible in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," she said.

She said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." The family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire.

A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said she plans to move her family out of the neighborhood. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. "Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me."

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: Large barn fire at Indiantown ranch closes roads, prompts horse evacuations
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue and Martin County Sheriff's deputies are on the scene of a large-scale barn fire at a ranch near SW Allapattah Road in Indiantown. The fire broke out at around 5:30 p.m. Thursday. At least five vehicles are involved in the fire, and horses roaming in a nearby pasture have been relocated as a precaution. No injuries have been reported at this time.

The blaze prompted emergency crews to close multiple roads in the immediate area to ensure public safety and allow firefighters access to battle the flames. Martin County Fire Rescue closed Allapattah Road at SW Palomino Street and Allapattah Road at SW Warfield Boulevard as a result of the fire. Drivers are being asked to avoid the area for the time being as crews continue working to extinguish the blaze.

The horse evacuations were necessary due to the proximity of the pasture to the burning barn. Officials relocated the animals to ensure their safety as the fire continued to burn. The extent of damage to the barn and the five vehicles has not yet been determined, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Crews remain on scene battling the fire. Additional details about the incident are expected to be released as the situation develops and investigators work to determine what sparked the blaze at the Indiantown ranch.

hero.headline: Data centers emerge as wedge issue in Florida's 2026 governor, Senate races
hero.body:
Data centers have become a defining issue in Florida's top 2026 races, with Democratic candidates calling for construction moratoriums and stronger regulation while Republicans emphasize investment and local control, as new polling shows a majority of Florida adults oppose large facilities in their own communities.

Democratic governor nominee David Jolly pledged to halt data center development temporarily if elected. In a campaign video filmed in Northern Virginia, Jolly described concerns about pollution, noise and neighborhood disruption near existing facilities and renewed his commitment to action. "I've proposed a one-year moratorium," Jolly said. "My first day in office as governor, I will issue that moratorium." Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Angie Nixon visited Fort Meade this week to hear residents' concerns about the large buildings that power artificial intelligence. "A lot of people are concerned with the environmental impacts and the health impacts of data centers coming into their neighborhoods," Nixon said. Nixon wants greater transparency around development decisions, stronger regulations and financial relief from developers if their projects hurt residents economically. She also raised concerns about potential increases in electricity and water bills.

Republican governor nominee Byron Donalds warned in an August interview that a statewide freeze could push investment elsewhere. "But you can't build for your life if you don't have a high-paying job," Donalds said. "And you're not going to have a high-paying job if you don't have companies who invest in your state." Donalds supports protections for water supplies and utility customers, cooling systems that conserve water and keeping facilities away from homes. In the Senate race, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody emphasized local and state decision-making. "It needs to be up to the people of a community or a state to decide what works best for them," Moody said.

A new Stetson University survey found 54% of Florida adults oppose large data centers in their own communities, compared with 27% who support them. The same survey shows both Republican nominees leading their Democratic opponents. Likely-voter estimates, including undecided respondents who leaned toward a candidate, put Donalds at 51% to Jolly's 39%. Moody received 51% to Nixon's 40%. The results do not establish how much data center policy is influencing candidate preferences. Democratic legislative candidates also are calling for a pause, tying the issue to their affordability agenda. "They have broken trust with the voters," said Richard Lamondin, the Democratic nominee for Florida Senate District 38, referring to state leaders. Stetson surveyed 830 Florida adults through an online panel in September. hero.headline: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. 1, the first increase since 2011. Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain at $200 per violation.

Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would encourage motorists to abide by the regulations. Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city.

"We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move," Kerensky said. "It creates turnover and can benefit from that."

Residents expressed mixed reactions to the change. Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, said she has been tagged multiple times for not moving after two hours. Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to.

"There's only so much parking, and it's usually on a beach day here, it's very [full] there's enough cars here that it's almost impossible," Wapnick said.

Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work.

"You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they're going to get their money anyway," Billero said.

Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate, with property taxes on the ballot this November.

"I think we did it at the opportune time," Cotugno said. "Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress."

Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions.

"I think that's something that possibly should come up for discussion," Cotugno said.

Parking in Vero Beach is free, but the increased fines will apply to violations of posted time limits and other parking regulations.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce community rallies for brothers killed in Georgia shooting; suspect charged
hero.teaser: The Fort Pierce community is raising money through GoFundMe to bring home two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday in Georgia. An 18-year-old suspect has been arrested and charged in connection with their deaths.
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce community is rallying around a grieving family through donations and other support after two young brothers were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark home to Florida to be laid to rest.

The boys grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt said both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother said they did everything together as a family and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family.

DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. The shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier, according to police. The mother of the two boys said the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired.

Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said no family should have to endure the senseless loss of children. Cochran-Johnson added that no mother or father should have to bury their children.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings targeting homes, suspects identified
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Officers responded to one home around 9:07 p.m. Friday and found multiple bullet holes outside, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. At least 10 bullet holes were visible in the front of the home. Bullets entered a teenage son's bedroom. The mother said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. The family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire.

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The teen said she was outside when the gunfire erupted and tried to run inside. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," she said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: Fort Lauderdale woman makes first court appearance in stolen Broward Sheriff's cruiser case
cards.teaser: Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, appeared in court Wednesday after she was arrested Tuesday night when authorities found a stolen Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car abandoned on I-95 in St. Lucie County. She faces nine charges across two counties.
cards.body:
Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, made her first court appearance Wednesday after she was arrested Tuesday night in connection with a stolen Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car that was abandoned on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The Fort Lauderdale woman now faces nine charges across two counties.

Dillon faces seven charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces two charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft.

The incident began at 9:30 p.m. Tuesday when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard.

Florida Highway Patrol located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Dillon in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

cards.headline: Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce launches diocese's first full special-needs program
cards.teaser: Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program Thursday, the first program in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs.
cards.body:
Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program Thursday morning with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, marking the first program of its kind in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs. The program began as a pilot in August with seven students.

Bishop Manuel de Jesus Rodriguez of the Diocese of Palm Beach attended the ceremony and interacted with students. "It's the first of its kind, offering full experience of Catholic education to children with special needs," Rodriguez said.

The Rev. Principal Kevin Hoeffner said the school previously struggled to accommodate students with special needs. "So, I've been here 20 years here at St. Anastasia, and unfortunately, we've had to either let students go when they can't make it past a certain grade, or they come in the front door, and they really want a Catholic education, and we unable to provide that for them," Hoeffner said. He added that the program aims to support families raising children with special needs. "My gosh, right now, parents are having a hard time raising a special need. Sometimes they can feel alone and isolated. So, it's nice that we can open our doors to them and be able to offer the tools and resources for them, not only to assist them but also for them to understand the faith," he said.

The Morning Star program includes sensory-friendly classrooms, a modified curriculum, small class sizes and individualized learning plans tailored to each student. The school hopes to expand the program to help more students and families in the community. Thursday's launch also marks the school's 100 years of Catholic education in Fort Pierce.

hero.headline: Martin County first responders rescue man after jump into St. Lucie River
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue, the Martin County Sheriff's Office and the Stuart Police Department worked together Wednesday night to rescue a man in a mental health crisis who jumped into the St. Lucie River.

Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to an attempted suicide at 10:18 p.m. Wednesday near Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard. A man jumped off West Bridge into the low tide water of the St. Lucie River, a Martin County Fire Rescue spokesperson confirmed Thursday.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Stuart Police Department officers searched the river using their boats. Martin County Sheriff's Office personnel located the man and transported him in their boat to a nearby boat ramp.

The man was conscious and breathing when paramedics assisted him. A LifeStar helicopter transported the man to a hospital with traumatic injuries.

Anyone who needs help can talk with the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or by chatting online. The 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast can be reached by dialing 211 or by texting a ZIP code to 898211.

hero.headline: Amendment 3 could force Florida to itemize tax bills by service
hero.body:
Florida cities and counties could begin billing residents separately for individual services if Amendment 3 passes, which would require local governments to unbundle property tax bills. One former state senator warns the change could transform property tax statements into itemized lists of charges for services such as sheriff and fire departments.

Former Florida State Sen. Brandes said most cities and counties will likely turn their sheriffs and fire departments into non-ad valorem taxes and create districts around those services. Individuals will see those services as separate line items on their tax bills.

Brandes compared the shift to the difference between buying a ticket on United Airlines and buying a ticket from Spirit Airlines. Things are bundled up on a United ticket but broken out on a Spirit ticket with every service listed separately. He said Florida is headed toward the Spirit Airlines model of tax bills.

Leaders in cities and counties have been discussing the impact of Amendment 3 all summer and how to adjust to finding new funding. Questions have arisen about whether separate entities already on property tax bills, such as the South Florida Water Management District, will send each homeowner individual bills.

Leaders in cities and counties have been discussing all summer the impact of Amendment 3 and how to adjust to finding new funding. The email from Stephanie wondered, "Are those gonna be separate entities that send each homeowner a bill?" I recently talked with former Florida State Sen. cards.headline: Data centers emerge as defining 2026 campaign issue as Stetson poll finds majority opposition
cards.teaser: A new Stetson University survey found 54% of Florida adults oppose large data centers in their own communities, and Democratic gubernatorial and Senate candidates are calling for construction pauses while Republican nominees emphasize investment and local input.
cards.body:
Data centers have become a central debate in Florida's 2026 gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races, with candidates staking out sharply contrasting positions as new polling shows most adults oppose the facilities in their neighborhoods.

A Stetson University survey found 54% of Florida adults oppose large data centers in their own communities, compared with 27% who support them. Stetson surveyed 830 Florida adults through an online, nonprobability panel in September. The university reported margins of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points for the adult results and 4.3 points for its estimates weighted for likely turnout.

Democratic governor nominee David Jolly is making the issue part of his campaign. In a campaign video filmed in Northern Virginia, Jolly described concerns about pollution, noise and neighborhood disruption near existing facilities. He renewed his pledge to halt development temporarily in Florida. "I've proposed a one-year moratorium," Jolly said. "My first day in office as governor, I will issue that moratorium."

Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Angie Nixon brought the debate to Fort Meade this week, visiting a traditionally Republican area to hear residents' concerns. "A lot of people are concerned with the environmental impacts and the health impacts of data centers coming into their neighborhoods," Nixon said. Nixon wants greater transparency around development decisions, stronger regulations and financial relief from developers if their projects hurt residents economically. She also raised concerns about potential increases in electricity and water bills.

Republican governor nominee Byron Donalds warned in an August interview that a statewide freeze could push investment elsewhere. He argued that attracting businesses and jobs is part of addressing affordability. "But you can't build for your life if you don't have a high-paying job," Donalds said. "And you're not going to have a high-paying job if you don't have companies who invest in your state." Donalds supports protections for water supplies and utility customers, cooling systems that conserve water and keeping facilities away from homes.

In the Senate race, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody has emphasized local and state decision-making. "It needs to be up to the people of a community or a state to decide what works best for them," Moody said.

Democratic legislative candidates also are calling for a pause, tying the issue to their affordability agenda and residents' ability to influence development decisions. "They have broken trust with the voters," said Richard Lamondin, the Democratic nominee for Florida Senate District 38, referring to state leaders. Lamondin argued Tallahassee has weakened residents' ability to have a say in what gets built in their communities.

The Stetson survey shows both Republican nominees leading their Democratic opponents. Its likely-voter estimates, including undecided respondents who leaned toward a candidate, put Donalds at 51% to Jolly's 39%. Moody received 51% to Nixon's 40%. Those results do not establish how much data-center policy is influencing candidate preferences.

hero.headline: Martin County first responders rescue man from St. Lucie River after jump from West Bridge
hero.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue, the Sheriff's Office, and Stuart Police Department worked together late Wednesday to rescue a man who jumped from West Bridge into the St. Lucie River during a mental health crisis.
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue, the Sheriff's Office, and Stuart Police Department worked together late Wednesday to rescue a man who jumped from West Bridge into the St. Lucie River during a mental health crisis.

Fire Rescue units responded to an attempted suicide at 10:18 p.m. Wednesday near Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard, according to a Fire Rescue spokesperson. The man jumped off West Bridge into low tide water.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Stuart Police Department officers searched the river using their boats. Sheriff's Office personnel located the man and transported him in their boat to a nearby boat ramp.

The man was conscious and breathing when paramedics assisted him, the Fire Rescue spokesperson said. A LifeStar helicopter took the man to a hospital with traumatic injuries.

Anyone experiencing a mental health crisis can talk with the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988, or chatting online. The 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast is available by dialing 211 or texting a ZIP code to 898211.

cards.headline: Martin County High sophomore arrested for bomb threat, fourth at school in 10 days
cards.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School sophomore was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat to skip class, the fourth threat against the school in just over a week, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators are still pursuing the other three threats and may make additional arrests.

The student, identified as Noah Taylor in earlier reports, submitted the false threat through the Fortify Florida app around 9 a.m. Tuesday, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to Budensiek. The tip claimed someone overheard students in the boys bathroom talking about bombs that would explode during third period, including one in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators traced the electronic submission back to Taylor using security camera footage. He initially denied involvement and suggested someone else sent the tip, but later confessed and explained he just wanted to get out of third-period class, Budensiek said. Taylor was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services facility in Fort Pierce.

Budensiek confirmed Tuesday's arrest is not connected to the three other recent threats against the school. The first threat came through Russia, he said, and investigators are still working the last two cases with potential arrests pending. The sheriff warned students that bomb threats carry catastrophic consequences including felony charges, potential expulsion, and lasting employment difficulties. The incidents have occurred just six weeks into the academic year.

hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie voters to decide local ballot questions Nov. 3 on land, taxes, trash
hero.body:
Voters in Martin and St. Lucie counties will decide five local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from land protection and mosquito control to sales taxes and trash pickup.

In Martin County, two questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve.

St. Lucie County has three local issues. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. 1, 2028. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work.

Port St. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee. The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents' preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change.

The third St. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy.

The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments.

hero.headline: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first increase since 2011
hero.body:
Vero Beach will double most parking fines starting Oct. 1, marking the first increase since 2011. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to raise fines for timed parking violations from $20 to $40 and other miscellaneous infractions from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain $200 per violation.

Vero Beach police requested the rate increase in a letter to the City Council in August, saying it would encourage motorists to abide by regulations. Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. "We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move," Kerensky said. "It creates turnover and can benefit from that."

The change drew mixed reactions from residents and business owners who cited limited parking availability. Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, said she has been tagged multiple times for not moving after two hours. Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. "There's only so much parking, and it's usually on a beach day here, it's very full, there's enough cars here that it's almost impossible," Wapnick said.

Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, suggested a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. Mayor John Cotugno acknowledged the timing of the fine increase coincides with property taxes on the ballot this November. "I think we did it at the opportune time," Cotugno said. "Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress." Cotugno said the city may explore permit options and other long-term parking solutions.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested under hotel bed faces meth, child neglect charges
hero.teaser: Kenneth Robert Ferow II, wanted on a Martin County battery warrant, was arrested at a Village Parkway hotel where police found him hiding under a bed with methamphetamine and two children in the room.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested Kenneth Robert Ferow II on methamphetamine possession and child neglect charges after finding the 41-year-old hiding under a bed at a Village Parkway hotel where he was wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant. Officers discovered two children, ages 14 and 8, inside the hotel room.

Police went to the hotel on Tuesday after receiving information that Ferow was inside a room. His wife told officers he was not there. Officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room.

Officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there. They ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident.

Officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine. Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding Martin County warrant.

cards.headline: Three shootings on Avenue L in Fort Pierce linked and targeted, police say
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police confirmed that three separate shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects.

The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Police say evidence shows all three shootings are related.

"The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

One Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep."

A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said she now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said.

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

cards.headline: Multi-agency response recovers stolen Broward deputy car on I-95 in Port St. Lucie, woman faces 9 charges
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie Police, Florida Highway Patrol, and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office worked together to locate and recover a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along I-95 near Gatlin Boulevard Tuesday night. Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale was arrested and faces nine criminal charges.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police, Florida Highway Patrol, and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office worked together to locate and recover a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard Tuesday night. Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale was arrested and faces nine criminal charges including grand theft of law enforcement equipment and possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon.

Broward County Regional Communications received a report shortly after 9 p.m. that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.

Deputies spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the department deployed both K-9 units and drone resources. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident.

Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The Broward County Sheriff's Office stated that nothing is missing from the vehicle and the Internal Affairs Unit is investigating to determine what happened and if any agency policy was violated. The deputy was on duty when he reported his marked unit missing.

hero.headline: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first increase since 2011
hero.body:
Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. 1, the first increase since 2011. Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain at $200 per violation.

Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would encourage motorists to abide by the regulations. Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. Parking in Vero Beach is free, but Kerensky said officials needed to give drivers an incentive to move and create turnover.

Residents pushed back on the increase, citing limited parking availability. Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. On beach days, he said, parking is almost impossible. Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, said she has been ticketed multiple times for not moving her vehicle after two hours.

Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. He suggested the city could charge a monthly permit fee. Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate, coming as property taxes appear on the ballot this November. Cotugno said the city had to readdress fees and left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions.

hero.headline: Sebastian River High School gets new play clocks after 17 businesses raise $10,000
hero.body:
Seventeen local businesses raised more than $10,000 to buy new play clocks for Sebastian River High School's varsity football program, replacing worn-out equipment that had plagued the team for years.

Coach Phinehas Weatherly said equipment failures made it difficult to run an effective offense for the past four years. Each repair cost thousands of dollars, a price the high school football program struggled to keep up with.

"For the last four years, it's been a battle of trying to get a working play clock, which is essential when you're trying to run an offense and keep it moving and not get delay games," Weatherly said.

Weatherly turned to Facebook for help. Shark alum Bryan Rhoades saw the post and took action, sharing his own video online asking the community to step up. Rhoades owns Airbnbs in the area along with River Ride Cart Rentals LLC. He offered to donate $1,000 and encouraged other businesses to do the same.

"Within like an hour I had $2,000 and within I think three more days we had $10,350," Rhoades said.

The old play clocks were stationary and had suffered significant wear and tear over the years, requiring repeated electrical repairs and parts replacements. The new clocks are lit up, bright, and roll around so they can be kept out of the weather.

"For the longest time, it seemed like we were just getting pushed to the side. And to see that there's people out there that still care and want to support and want to help, you know, it was great. It was amazing," Weatherly said.

Rhoades said the outpouring of support reflected the character of the Sebastian community.

"Everybody is out there still trying to help each other, still willing to give and be part of the community and make things better for the kids," Weatherly said.

The new play clocks are expected to debut at Sebastian River's next home football game in October.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police find Martin County warrant fugitive hiding under hotel bed
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie police arrested a man wanted on a Martin County battery warrant after finding him hiding under a bed at a hotel on Village Parkway. Officers also found methamphetamine on him and two children in the room.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested Kenneth Robert Ferow II, 41, after finding him hiding under a bed at a hotel on Village Parkway on Tuesday. Ferow was wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant.

Officers went to the hotel after receiving information that Ferow was inside a room. Ferow's wife told officers he was not there, but officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room.

Officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there. Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident.

Officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine. Two children, ages 14 and 8, were also inside the hotel room. Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding warrant.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings, identify suspects as families plan to leave
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three separate shootings that struck homes on Avenue L between September 15 and September 18 are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. One home hit by gunfire sheltered a mother and her four children inside, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom.

The shootings occurred Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three incidents are related through similar means, methods and weapons. Police responded to one home around 9:07 p.m. Friday and found multiple bullet holes outside, with several rounds penetrating walls and windows. At least 10 bullet holes marked the front of that home, which was struck three times within days.

The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. Her teenage son narrowly escaped being hit in his bedroom. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also struck by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl living next door said she was outside when gunfire erupted and fell to the ground as she tried to run inside. A bullet entered the house where she would have been standing.

Santiago said the targeted homes and people involved have histories that investigators are using to develop the case and build probable cause. The mother whose home was repeatedly hit said she plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. No one was injured in any of the shootings. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive.

hero.headline: 17 businesses raise over $10,000 for Sebastian River High play clocks after coach's Facebook post
hero.body:
Seventeen local businesses raised more than $10,000 for new play clocks at Sebastian River High School after coach Phinehas Weatherly posted about equipment problems on Facebook.

Weatherly said the varsity football program has struggled with malfunctioning play clocks for four years. Each repair cost thousands of dollars.

"For the last four years, it's been a battle of trying to get a working play clock, which is essential when you're trying to run an offense and keep it moving and not get delay games," Weatherly said.

Weatherly made a Facebook post saying the situation was ridiculous and that the school could not get basic equipment while other schools received more support. Sebastian River alum Bryan Rhoades saw the post and shared his own video online asking the community to help.

"I need five business owners or people, whoever, to match my $1,000. We can get this done," Rhoades said.

Rhoades owns Airbnbs in the area and River Ride Cart Rentals LLC. The response was swift.

"Within like an hour I had $2,000 and within I think three more days we had $10,350," Rhoades said.

The old play clocks were stationary and had suffered significant wear and tear over the years, requiring repeated electrical repairs and parts replacements. The new clocks are lit up, bright and roll around so they can be kept out of the weather.

"For the longest time, it seemed like we were just getting pushed to the side. And to see that there's people out there that still care and want to support and want to help, you know, it was great. It was amazing," Weatherly said.

Rhoades said the support reflected the character of the Sebastian community.

"They just want to get out there and help. That's what it comes down to really. You know what I mean, the kids," Rhoades said.

The new play clocks are expected to debut at Sebastian River's next home football game in October.

hero.headline: Brightline expected to file bankruptcy, casting doubt on Stuart station
hero.body:
Brightline is expected to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week to restructure about $5.5 billion in debt, according to financial media outlets including Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal. The rail line plans to keep its trains running on schedule despite the filing. The expected bankruptcy raises new questions about the long-delayed Stuart station project and future Treasure Coast rail service.

Brightline selected Stuart as its designated Treasure Coast stop more than two years ago, but project timelines and cost-sharing agreements have remained a frequent topic of debate. The proposed station in downtown Stuart has faced a winding road of funding discussions, local debates and regional planning.

The company reported in June that total ridership was 292,339, up 15 percent year-over-year, with average daily ridership of 9,745. Brightline has been offering service from South Florida to Orlando for the past three years, a massive expansion project that cost the company $6 billion and took four years to complete.

Brightline's June ridership report also mentioned that the company still plans to construct a station in Cocoa and to extend the rail system from Orlando to Tampa.

hero.headline: Arsenic hot spot found on Fort Pierce brownfield, not Shelli development site
hero.body:
New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the waterfront parcel the city sold to developer Chris Shelli, raising questions about the city's earlier claim that contamination could wipe out his damages in an ongoing lawsuit.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection found arsenic about 148 times the residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of a former citrus packing house property immediately north of Fisherman's Wharf. St. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site. On the approximately 3.2-acre development parcel the city sold to Shelli, FDEP found arsenic above residential cleanup targets in only two soil samples, both less than twice the target level.

The city sent Shelli a letter in 2025 arguing the property was likely contaminated and that the cost of remediation essentially eliminates his damages claim. The city made that assertion before FDEP completed its testing. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels associated with the former citrus packing house property but did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.

Jordan Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, reviewed the findings and said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. Beckler said the vast majority of the samples were not that high above the residential standard and noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils.

Shelli sued Fort Pierce for breach of contract after emails showed city commissioners did not learn until 2023, about two years after the sale, that removing a state right-of-reverter restriction on roughly half the property could cost nearly $2 million. The restriction means the land could revert to the state if sold for private development.

Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, said questions could remain over what the city knew or should have known and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before purchase.

Fort Pierce commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli in March. The city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action and the offer was later deemed rejected.

Mike Jenkins, whose family owns the property beneath 12A Buoy restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf and has owned the property for roughly 50 years, said associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. A city spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.

resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. cards.headline: Parking dispute sparked Pollo Tropical shooting in Port St. Lucie, police say
cards.teaser: Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details.
cards.body:
Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details that show the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space.

Multiple witnesses told police they observed Harris push another man and engage in a verbal argument before the man discharged a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris came back inside the restaurant and asked someone to call 911.

A witness picking up an Uber order told police she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot.

A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to come outside. The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris ran up on him with a knife.

Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed that Harris, listed as a victim in the report, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three shootings on Avenue L, say suspects identified
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L over four days are connected and targeted. A mother and her four children were inside one home when bullets entered, including rounds that hit her teenage son's bedroom.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects.

The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep."

The family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire.

A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said she now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. "Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me."

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: Fire at Wendy's on Jensen Beach Boulevard caused by burned-out AC fan motor
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to a fire at a Wendy's restaurant at 1409 NE Jensen Beach Boulevard in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon. The fire was caused by a burned-out fan motor in an air conditioning unit on the roof. The building was safely evacuated, no injuries were reported, and no nearby structures were threatened.

Units were called to the scene at around 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday after reports of smoke and visible flames coming from inside the restaurant, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The emergency call brought firefighters to the location to investigate the source of the smoke and flames that had been reported by witnesses at the scene.

Upon arrival, firefighters found white smoke coming from the AC unit on the roof and light to moderate smoke inside the building. Crews worked to locate the source of the fire and discovered it was the air conditioning unit mounted on the roof of the restaurant. After inspecting the unit, firefighters noticed the fan motor had burned out, which was determined to be the cause of the fire and smoke.

Martin County Fire Rescue successfully extinguished the fire and ensured the building was safe before clearing the scene. The quick response by fire crews prevented the fire from spreading to other parts of the building or threatening nearby structures in the area. No firefighters or civilians were injured during the incident, and the evacuation of the building proceeded without complications.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast voters face local ballot questions Nov. 3 on taxes, services, land
hero.body:
Treasure Coast voters will decide five local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from land protection and mosquito control to sales taxes and trash pickup.

In Martin County, two proposed charter amendments apply only to Stuart voters. One would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve.

St. Lucie County has three local issues. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Port St. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee. The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents' preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change.

A third St. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy.

No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River County. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments.
